summary: Proposes conventions for using an IBM 2741 typewriter-style terminal to log in to ARPANET server hosts. The 2741 can key in 92 different codes, but a few of them, such as the cent sign and the new-line key, have no direct ASCII equivalent, so the note suggests how to map them. RFC 135 responded with a different set of conventions.

plainLanguage.summary: A special typewriter has fewer keys than the character code used by computers, so some characters cannot be typed at all. This note agrees on a prefix key and a set of key combinations that fill the gaps.

subtitle: How to type every ASCII character from a typewriter-style IBM 2741 terminal when logging in to ARPANET server hosts.

tldr.problem: An IBM 2741 terminal can key only 92 codes, so it cannot produce all 128 ASCII codes that server hosts expect: 7 ASCII graphics and 31 ASCII controls are missing, and its cent sign and New Line key have no ASCII code of their own.
tldr.mechanism: The note chooses one escape character and a few single-key functions, then pairs the escape character with other keys to stand in for each missing graphic and control code.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposed set of conventions rather than a standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 135 as an update to it.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 110 the status unknown and lists RFC 135 as an update to it. The document itself is a set of recommended conventions from March 1971.

sections.title: The 2741 Terminal Problem
sections.content:
An IBM 2741 terminal can key in 92 different codes: 88 graphics plus the four controls SP, BS, HT and NL. Each of these has a defined ASCII code except the cent graphic and the New Line control.

When NL is keyed, the program receiving the keyboard input can translate that signal into whichever line end the host in use needs: NL, CR or LF.
sections.plainLanguage: The terminal has fewer keys than the language computers use, and a few of its keys do not match any character. Something has to fill the gap.

sections.title: What Has to Be Keyable
sections.content:
Seven ASCII graphics and 31 ASCII controls cannot be keyed on a 2741, so some way is needed to reach all 128 ASCII codes. The note requires one character to be chosen as an escape (prefix) character that, together with the characters after it, converts into any desired ASCII code.

Three other functions are usually shown by a single key. Character delete removes this character and the one before it. Line delete removes this character and every earlier character in the current line. Logical line end is treated as if NL were entered, so one physical line can hold several logical lines.

A system escape character is also needed, so that keyed text can be read by the user program instead of being sent to the Server Host. Lines read that way are not sent onward. A user program may also need to send the INS or INR network control commands, either after the system escape character or through the attention button on the terminal, depending on the user's operating system.
sections.plainLanguage: The plan needs one prefix key that marks the next keys as special, plus keys for erasing one character, erasing a whole line, and ending a line early.

sections.title: Recommended Special Characters
sections.content:
The note recommends specific characters for the special functions. Because the cent sign and the logical NOT sign are not ASCII, the text writes them as $CENT and $NOT.

  • Character escape: $NOT
  • System escape: |
  • Character delete: @
  • Line delete: $CENT
  • Logical line end: #

The system escape also lets a user give other commands to the user program, such as suppressing or restoring typeout of received messages, directing received messages or keyed input to a disk file, or aborting the user program.
sections.plainLanguage: The note gives each job to a key: one is the prefix, one erases a character, one erases a line, and one lets you talk to your own program instead of the distant host.

sections.title: Escape Pairs for the Missing Codes
sections.content:
For the seven missing ASCII graphics, the recommendation is the character escape followed by one key: $NOT < gives [, $NOT > gives ], $NOT ( gives {, $NOT ) gives }, $NOT / gives \ and $NOT ' gives `. The double-quote key after the escape gives ^.

The special function characters can be keyed the same way, for example $NOT - for $NOT, $NOT : for | and $NOT = for #.

For the ASCII controls, the character escape is followed by two letters taken from the control's mnemonic. Examples are $NOT BE for BEL (X'07') and $NOT ES for ESC (X'1B'). The controls SP, BS and HT can be keyed either directly or with the escape.
sections.plainLanguage: To type a missing symbol you press the prefix key and then a stand-in key. To type a missing control you press the prefix key and two letters that spell its name.

items.label: Character escape
items.desc: Prefix that turns the following characters into any ASCII code.

items.label: System escape
items.desc: Sends keyed text to the user program instead of the host.

items.label: Character delete
items.desc: Deletes this character and the one before it.

items.label: Line delete
items.desc: Deletes this character and all earlier ones in the line.

items.label: Logical line end
items.desc: Ends a logical line as if NL were entered.
